findings.text: Mutex release first releases lock dependency tracking for the caller return context and then releases the underlying real-time mutex base object.
Real-time mutex unlock attempts a release compare exchange from current holder to empty as a fast path and only enters the slow unlock routine when that exchange does not succeed.

Two build variants exist for the release exchange on the owner field: one performs an atomic release exchange and reports its outcome, the other unconditionally reports failure and thereby forces all unlocks into the slow path.

Slow unlock holds the wait lock with interrupts saved, then either repeatedly attempts a safe empty transition while no waiters are present or, when waiters exist, queues the highest priority waiter for deferred wakeup, releases the wait lock, and drains the wake queue.

Safe unlock has fast-path and serialized variants. The fast-path form snapshots the owner, clears the waiters indication while holding the wait lock, drops that lock, then attempts a release exchange to empty and signals retry on failure. The serialized form stores empty while holding the wait lock and always reports success.

Clearing the owner under the wait lock without the exchange window can race with concurrent fast-path acquire and object freeing after wait-lock release, so the fast-path form preserves correctness by clearing the waiters mark under the lock and completing ownership release with an atomic exchange afterwards.

Manipulation of the waiters indication requires holding the wait lock. Slow unlock uses interrupt-saving acquisition to support early boot callers, and safe unlock releases that lock before reporting its result.

Selection of the next waiter requires holding the wait lock and additionally acquires the current task priority-inheritance lock. It dequeues the top waiter from the current priority chain, re-evaluates current priority, leaves a waiters-only owner marker so newcomers take the slow path, disables preemption, and defers the actual wakeup until after the wait lock is released.

Deferred wakeup distinguishes a special real-time lock wait state from ordinary wakeups. The special waiter is reference counted and held in a dedicated single slot, while other tasks join a generic wake queue. Draining wakes the special task with its dedicated state and drops the reference, drains the generic queue, and re-enables preemption paired with the earlier disable.
A real-time wake-queue head aggregates a generic wake-queue head plus a nullable dedicated task pointer for the special real-time lock waiter, initialized empty by its definition macro.

Debug helpers are inert unless real-time mutex debugging is enabled, in which case they poison a newly initialized waiter and warn when unlock or proxy unlock observes an unexpected owner relationship.

Futex queue insertion increments the bucket waiter count before acquiring the bucket spinlock so a concurrent waker cannot miss a task that is about to sleep, records the bucket lock in the queue entry, then takes that spinlock. The error unwind path decrements the count and releases the bucket lock when the entry is not queued.

Queued futex waiters are ordered by capped priority: real-time priorities retain their order while all non-real-time threads share the maximum real-time priority value and therefore retire in insertion order after real-time waiters.

A queue entry lock pointer may change concurrently, so removal and lock acquisition read it once, acquire the observed spinlock under read-copy-update protection, revalidate that the pointer is unchanged, and retry on mismatch. Successful removal asserts absence of priority-inheritance state and reports whether an entry was detached.

Direct hash-bucket removal requires holding the entry recorded lock, detaches the priority-list node from its bucket chain, and decrements the bucket waiter count. The priority-inheritance removal form is conditional because an unlocker may already have dequeued the entry in the window between real-time mutex release and bucket locking, then it releases the associated inheritance state and clears the pointer.

Priority-inheritance state is reference counted. Release is inert for null or non-final references. The final release, when an owner remains, clears ownership under the inheritance mutex wait lock through a proxy unlock, then either frees the object when the caller already has a cached object or recycles it as the caller cache after clearing owner and restoring the count.

Ownership transfer of inheritance state requires holding the inheritance mutex wait lock and nests each involved task priority-inheritance lock separately: detach from the old owner list under the old task lock and attach to the new owner list under the new task lock.
Proxy unlock only clears encoded ownership while the caller holds the wait lock, relying on the subsequent wait-lock release for release ordering.
Robust handling distinguishes a pending-operation mode from a list-traversal mode through two boolean constants.

Robust futex death handling rejects unaligned addresses, loads the user word with fault and contention retries, and checks ownership by thread identifier. A non-owner with a pending non-inheritance operation wakes one waiter when the word appears unlocked or owned without waiters indicated. A true owner atomically preserves the waiters indication while marking owner death, retries on concurrent change, and wakes one waiter for non-inheritance futexes when waiters were indicated; inheritance futex wakeup is left to task exit handling.
Locked user compare exchange disables page faults around an inatomic user compare exchange and always re-enables faults before returning its status.

Futex wake validates a non-empty bitset, resolves the futex key for reading, performs robust unlock processing first, honors a strict zero-count fast return, exits early when no bucket waiters are pending, then under the bucket lock scans matching entries, rejects entries carrying inheritance or real-time waiter state, skips entries with no bitset overlap, invokes each selected entry wake callback until the requested count is reached, and finally drains deferred wakeups and returns the woken count or error.
Pending-waiter detection uses a full memory barrier and an atomic waiter count on multiprocessor builds and unconditionally reports possible waiters on uniprocessor builds.

Robust unlock requested by flags first release-stores zero to the user futex word and then clears the caller pending-list word, reporting failure on user access fault. Clearing selects native or compatibility layouts from build width and robust-list size flags.

If clearing the user pending word faults and the faulting address aliases the current robust-list head pending field, the implementation discards the current robust-list pointer to avoid further corruption on task exit.
Robust list traversal reads one user list-link word and splits it into an entry pointer and modifier bits using the robust modifier mask.
